description: Dead hang to chin over the bar, no swing, no kick. Your strict pull-up number is the purest test of the cables that run from your fingers to your lats. Here is the honest test, what your reps reveal, and the five mistakes that build aching elbows instead of a back that pulls.

scenes.narration: Grab the bar | overhand, | just outside shoulders. | Hang completely still. | Arms fully straight. | That is the start | of every rep. | Pull your chin | clearly over the bar. | Lower back down | to a dead hang. | Pause. | Then pull again. | No swinging. | No kicking. | No chin reaching. | Count every strict rep | until you cannot | clear the bar. | That number | is your pull-up max. | Write it down. | At the end, | I will show you | the chain of cables | this number grades, | from your fingers | to your back.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN CLIMBING AND PULLING
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Ten strict pull-ups is where climbing the bar becomes pulling. If your number today is zero, you are standing at the most common starting line in calisthenics, and the path up from zero is the best-mapped road in bodyweight training. One to four means the chain is connected and every link is waking up. Five to nine means real pulling strength is under construction. Over fifteen strict, you own a back and a set of cables that most gym members never build, because machines let their weakest links hide. Understand what strictness did here. Every rep started from a dead hang and ended with a full lower, which means your number cannot be inflated by momentum or half reps. It is a pure reading of the chain. Pure readings are the only ones worth tracking.
scenes.sub: 0-2: cables untrained - over 15: serious pull power

scenes.narration: Trace one pull-up through the body and you will understand this test. Your fingers close on the bar, powered by forearm muscles through long tendons. The forearm pulls across the elbow, where the biceps and brachialis tendons bend the arm. The elbow hands the load to the lats, the huge wings of the back, which drag your whole body upward. Four links, one chain, and the chain can only ever be as strong as its least-trained link. For most beginners, the surprise is where it fails. The back is rarely the problem. The grip slips or the elbows fade first, because those smaller cables have carried less load across a lifetime than the big back muscles have. This is why your pull-up number is really a report card on the small links. Build them, and the number climbs even before the back itself gets much stronger. Ignore them, and the number stalls no matter how many rows you do.

lines: Every beginner's bridge to rep one.
beats.title: THE NEGATIVE

scenes.narration: Here is the training science inside the test. The dead hang at the bottom of every rep is not a rest. It is the moment the lat and elbow tendons are stretched under your full bodyweight, and that loaded stretch is a powerful building signal. Cut the rep short at the bottom and you delete the signal. Rush through it and you halve it. This is also why slow negatives, lowering yourself over five full seconds, are the classic bridge to a first pull-up. The lowering phase loads the same cables at a level you can already handle, and tendons rebuild eagerly from that dose. Every serious puller you have ever seen was built on full ranges and patient negatives long before they were built on volume. The test and the training are the same movement. Only the intention changes.

One warning belongs in every pull-up conversation, and almost nobody gives it. The tendons around your elbow adapt more slowly than the muscles they serve. Your lats might feel ready for daily max attempts within a fortnight. Your elbow cables are on a clock of months, and they keep the score silently until they suddenly do not. This is the origin of the famous climber's and calisthenics elbow ache: strong muscles enthusiastically overloading slow tendons, session after session. The fix is not fear. The fix is rhythm. Hard pulling days separated by easy days, volume that climbs gradually, and variety in grip width so the load rotates across the tissues. Slow here does not mean stuck. Tendons that adapt slowly also keep their gains for years. You are building the most durable strength of your life. Let it take the time it takes.

beats.text: EVERY KILO LESS IS A KILO LESS

scenes.narration: Now your advantage, | and it is enormous. | The pull-up is | pure relative strength. | It does not ask | how much you lift. | It asks | how much of you | you can lift. | Every kilo less | is a kilo less | on every rep, | every set, | every session. | Heavy guys spend months | with bands and boxes | just to reach rep one. | You start closer, | recover faster, | and stack more volume | while they are still | learning to hang. | Fifteen strict pull-ups | is elite anywhere. | On a light frame, | it is simply | a matter of time.
Now pull with me. Strict reps inside the window, full lower every time, rest fully between rounds. Thirty seconds of work, ninety seconds of rest, four rounds. Own every rep. Go.

beats.text: CHIN REACHING IS NOT CHIN OVER
VARY THE GRIP, SPARE THE CABLES

scenes.narration: Here are the five mistakes destroying your lat and elbow tendons. First, swinging and kipping. Momentum reps inflate your number while the cables do less work, and the test becomes fiction. Second, reaching with your chin, craning your neck to fake the last inch instead of pulling your chest higher. Third, half lowering. If the elbows never straighten, the tendons never get their loaded stretch, and the bottom of your strength stays empty. Fourth, one grip width forever, which hammers the exact same elbow tissues every session until they complain. Rotate widths and the load rotates with them. Fifth, max attempts every day. Muscles forgive that schedule. Elbow tendons do not, and if your elbows ever ache for days after pulling, ease off, and if it persists, see a professional. The strict road is slower per week and faster per year.

So, your number. Zero to two: the chain is connecting, and negatives plus dead hangs will carry you to five faster than you believe. Three to nine: every link is building, and this is the band where weekly progress feels almost unfair. Ten to fourteen: you own real pulling strength, the kind that transfers to climbing, grappling and every sport that involves your own body. Fifteen and beyond: your chain is elite, and your work becomes slow load and perfect maintenance. Whatever your number is, put it in the comments. Just the number. In thirty days we hang from this same bar and pull again, and the chain will report its own progress. One more honest note: test on a fresh day, not after a back workout, because a tired chain lies about its true number and you deserve the real one.
Thirty days from now, same bar, same dead hang start, more reps. Subscribe so you do not miss the retest, and bring your chain. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 pull-up max Mistakes That Are Destroying Your lat and elbow tendons
